lessons.title: Points per possession
lessons.objective: Explain pace, offensive rating, defensive rating and net rating.

payload.prompt: A typical NBA team completes about how many possessions per game?

explanation.correct: In recent seasons a typical NBA team has about 99 to 100 possessions a game. That count is called pace, and it shifts a little from year to year.
explanation.incorrect: An NBA team has roughly 100 possessions a game in recent seasons. Pace is that count, and it tells you how fast a team plays, not how well.

payload.prompt: An elite NBA offense scores about how many points per 100 possessions?

explanation.correct: In recent seasons the league average has been around 114 to 115, and the best offenses reach about 120. Offensive ratings drift upward over time, so always compare a team to that season's league average.
explanation.incorrect: Recent league averages sit in the mid-110s, so an elite offense is around 120. The scale has crept upward over the years, which is why comparing to the league average matters.

payload.prompt: What does an offensive rating tell you?

options.text: Points scored per 100 possessions, however fast the team plays.
The total number of points scored in a game.
How many possessions the team has per game.

explanation.correct: Offensive rating is points per 100 possessions, so it takes speed out of the picture. A fast team and a slow team can be compared fairly, because both are measured per possession.
explanation.incorrect: Total points depend on how many possessions a team gets, and possessions per game is pace. Offensive rating divides the scoring by the possessions to measure efficiency.

payload.prompt: What is net rating?

options.text: Offensive rating minus defensive rating: the margin per 100 possessions.
The team's winning percentage.
The team's average margin of victory in games it won.

explanation.correct: Net rating is what a team scores per 100 possessions minus what it allows. A positive number means it outscores opponents, and a net rating of +5 or better marks a strong team, while champions are often higher.
explanation.incorrect: Net rating is not a record or a game-by-game margin. It is the gap between offensive rating and defensive rating, and it is a better guide to team strength than wins alone.

payload.prompt: Match each metric to what it measures.

pairs.definition: How many possessions a team has per game, or per 48 minutes. It shows how fast a team plays.
Points scored per 100 possessions, which measures efficiency regardless of pace.
Points allowed per 100 possessions. Lower is better.
Offensive rating minus defensive rating, the margin per 100 possessions.

distractorDefinitions: The total number of points scored in a season.
The average score margin in games won by the team.

explanation.summary: Pace is speed; ORtg is what they score; DRtg is what they allow; NetRtg is the difference.

payload.prompt: What does a defensive rating tell you?

options.text: Points allowed per 100 possessions by the defense, measuring how efficiently the team limits opponent scoring.
The total points allowed in a season by the team.
How many defensive possessions a team creates per game.

explanation.correct: Right. Defensive rating (DRtg) is points per 100 possessions allowed. A great defense is 105 or below; 110+ is poor.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Defensive rating is points per 100 possessions allowed. It shows how well the defense controls scoring.

lessons.title: Efficiency: eFG% and TS%
lessons.objective: Say why a three counts more in eFG% and what TS% adds.

payload.prompt: A player shoots 50% from the field overall (45% twos, 35% threes on equal attempts). What is their eFG%?

explanation.correct: Right. eFG% accounts for three-pointers being worth 50% more. The formula is (FG + 0.5*3P) / FGA. This player's eFG is around 49%.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. eFG% gives three-pointers extra credit. The formula is (FG + 0.5*3P) / FGA. This player's eFG is higher than raw FG% because of the threes.

payload.prompt: A player shoots 48% from the field, 35% from three, and 80% from the free-throw line. About what is their TS%?

explanation.correct: Around there. TS% (True Shooting) is (Points) / (2 × (FGA + 0.44×FTA)). It accounts for all three scoring methods. This player's TS is about 57-59%.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. TS% includes field goals, three-pointers, and free throws in one metric. The formula weights free-throw attempts by 0.44 to account for defensive fouls.

payload.prompt: Why do teams track eFG% instead of just FG%?

options.text: Because three-pointers are worth 50% more than two-pointers, so eFG% gives credit for threes and reflects true scoring efficiency.
Because it counts free throws.
Because it is easier to calculate.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Regular FG% treats a two and a three the same, which undervalues three-point shooting. eFG% fixes that: (FG + 0.5*3P) / FGA.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. eFG% weights three-pointers by 1.5× because they are worth 50% more points. It shows shooting efficiency more accurately than FG%.

payload.prompt: What does TS% (True Shooting) measure that eFG% does not?

options.text: Free-throw efficiency, combining field goals, three-pointers and free throws into a single scoring efficiency metric.
How often the player shoots threes.
The number of assists per game.

explanation.correct: Right. TS% is total points divided by (2 × (FGA + 0.44×FTA)). It includes free throws, which eFG% ignores. TS% is more complete.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. TS% adds free-throw efficiency to the eFG% picture. Formula: Points / (2 × (FGA + 0.44×FTA)). A 60% TS is elite.

payload.prompt: Why is a corner three often more efficient?
payload.template: A corner three is more efficient than a mid-range shot because of {{ep}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Expected points (xP) is average points per shot. A 35% three is 1.05 xP; a 48% two is 0.96 xP.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Expected points is what a shot yields on average. A 35% three outvalues a 48% two.

lessons.title: Usage and stars
lessons.objective: Explain usage rate, PER and what a star profile looks like.

payload.prompt: What is usage rate?

options.text: The percentage of team possessions a player uses with a shot, pass attempt resulting in an assist, or turnover.
How many minutes a player is on the court.
The player's shooting percentage.

explanation.correct: Right. Usage rate (USG%) shows what percentage of team possessions involve that player. Stars have 25-35% USG; role players 10-20%.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Usage rate is the percentage of team possessions a player uses (FGA + FTA + TOV). High scorers have high USG rates.

payload.prompt: PER (Player Efficiency Rating) measures what?

options.text: A player's per-minute efficiency relative to their team's efficiency, accounting for scoring, rebounds, assists, turnovers and fouls.
Only the player's point total per game.
How many possessions the player initiates.

explanation.correct: Exactly. PER is a composite efficiency rating: (league-average PER is ~15). A PER of 20 is All-Star level; 25+ is MVP level.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. PER combines points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks, turnovers and fouls into one per-minute rating. 15 is average.

payload.prompt: What do Win Shares estimate?

options.text: The number of team wins a player contributed to through their offensive and defensive play.
The player's salary relative to other players.
How many games a player starts.

explanation.correct: Right. Win Shares convert a player's stats into estimated wins added to the team. A star might contribute 6-8 wins; a role player 1-2.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Win Shares estimate how many wins a player's performance added to the team. They combine offensive and defensive contributions.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: His usage rate is too high for a role player.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: He is handling the ball and taking shots on too many possessions for his talent level, hurting team efficiency.
He plays too many minutes per game.
He is fouling too much.
He shoots free throws too often.

payload.translation: She is saying the role player is using too high a percentage of team possessions (high USG%), which suggests he is over-playing his role instead of moving the ball.

followUps.why: You recognize that high usage by a role player means too many shots and not enough ball movement.

followUps.line: The star should have more usage.
followUps.why: A good follow-up noting that stars should use a higher percentage of possessions.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: High usage rate means handling the ball a lot; role players should have low USG%, stars 25-35%.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: His PER is elite but he is not clicking in games.

payload.question: What is she noting?

options.text: His efficiency rating is very high (20+), but his intangible playoff impact or clutch performances do not match his regular-season stats.
His shooting form is bad.
He fouls too much.
He is tired from playing too long.

payload.translation: She is saying stats (PER) do not tell the whole story; despite high efficiency numbers, the player is not performing in close games or high-leverage moments.

followUps.line: Yeah, he's not playing winning basketball.
followUps.why: You recognize that stats and winning are not always aligned.

followUps.line: Maybe it is a sample-size thing.
followUps.why: A good follow-up considering whether a small game sample is skewing the perception.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: High PER does not always mean a player is performing in clutch moments or close games.

lessons.title: All-in-one metrics
lessons.objective: Decode BPM, VORP and the all-in-one stat family without a math degree.

payload.prompt: Match each advanced metric to what it means.

pairs.definition: Estimated points per 100 possessions a player adds via box-score stats.
Estimated wins a player's performance added vs. a replacement-level player.
The per-100-possession point swing when a player is on vs. off the court.

distractorDefinitions: How many points a player scores per game.
The percentage of possessions a player handles the ball.

explanation.summary: BPM is per-100-possession impact from box-score stats; VORP converts it to estimated wins; On-Off is the direct per-100 differential.

payload.prompt: What does a Box Plus-Minus (BPM) of +8 mean?

options.text: The team scores 8 more points per 100 possessions with that player on the court compared to the league average.
The player scored 8 more points than their average.
The team won 8 more games because of the player.

explanation.correct: Right. BPM of +8 means the team's offensive/defensive balance is 8 points per 100 possessions better with that player. Elite defense + good offense = high BPM.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. BPM is a per-100-possession rating. +8 BPM means the team has an 8-point advantage per 100 possessions with that player.

payload.prompt: Why is VORP (Value Over Replacement) useful?

options.text: It shows how much a player adds compared to a readily available backup, helping assess whether a player's contract is worth the cost.
It shows the player's jersey number.
It predicts which team will win the championship.

explanation.correct: Exactly. VORP compares a player to a replacement (journeyman backup). A star with +4 VORP adds 4 wins. A bench player with +0.5 VORP is a bargain.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. VORP estimates how many wins a player contributed vs. a replacement-level player. It is used to evaluate contracts and value.

payload.prompt: What is the danger of relying only on all-in-one metrics like BPM or PER?

options.text: They oversimplify complex play and miss context like defense against specific opponents, clutch performance, or intangibles like leadership.
They are too hard to understand.
They favor old players over new ones.

explanation.correct: Right. Stats cannot capture everything. A player's on-ball defense, communication, spacing gravity and playoff performance matter beyond BPM or PER.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. All-in-one metrics are useful but incomplete. They miss clutch moments, defense nuance and intangibles. Use them with the eye test.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Look at his on-off numbers, the team is way better with him.

payload.question: What is she showing you?

options.text: When that player is on the court, the team's per-100-possession point differential is much higher than when he is off.
He plays both offense and defense.
He is on the court for more minutes than other players.
His uniform is different colors.

payload.translation: She is using on-off data to show that the team plays better (scores and allows fewer points) when this player is in the game.

followUps.why: You recognize that large on-off differentials show a player's impact on team success.
A good follow-up asking whether defense and playmaking also contribute to the on-off number.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: On-Off differential is just how much better the team plays with that player in the game.

lessons.title: Shot charts
lessons.objective: Read a shot chart: hot zones, cold zones and the dead midrange.

payload.prompt: Tap the area where the most efficient three-pointer is shot (shortest distance).

diagram.alt: A basketball court showing the three-point line.

explanation.correct: Right! The corner three is the shortest distance at 22 ft in the NBA. Corner threes are the most efficient shot from distance.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The corner three is only 22 ft from the basket, the shortest three-point distance. That is why corner threes are so valuable.

payload.prompt: Tap the area where teams score the most efficiently (closest to the basket).

diagram.alt: A basketball court showing areas near the basket.

explanation.correct: Exactly! Shots at the rim (layups, dunks) have the highest efficiency, often 55-65% or more. This is the most valuable shot location.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Rim shots are the most efficient. Layups and dunks go in 55-65% of the time or higher, much better than midrange.

payload.prompt: Tap the area where teams shoot the fewest threes and score least efficiently (the dead midrange).

diagram.alt: A basketball court showing the midrange area.

explanation.correct: Right! The midrange (10-22 ft) is dead: low efficiency compared to rim shots and threes. Modern teams avoid it and shoot threes instead.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The midrange (10-22 ft) is the least valuable shot in modern basketball. It combines the low efficiency of distance with no three-point reward.

payload.prompt: A shot chart shows what?

options.text: Every shot a player or team took, where it was taken from, and whether it went in (often as a heat map of make rates by location).
Only the three-pointers a player attempted.
The order in which shots were taken during a game.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Shot charts map every shot. Made shots (usually green) and misses (usually red) show where a player or team is hot or cold.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Shot charts visualize all shots on a court diagram, showing makes and misses by location. Heat maps show efficiency by zone.

payload.prompt: Why did NBA analytics kill the midrange?

options.text: Midrange shots are less efficient than rim shots or threes. Teams avoid them.
Because guards do not like taking midrange shots.
Because defenders are better at those distances.

explanation.correct: Right. A 45% two-pointer (0.9 xP) is worth less than a 35% three (1.05 xP). Teams prefer high-volume threes and close rim shots.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Analytics show rim shots and threes produce more expected points than midrange. Teams intentionally avoided the midrange in recent years.

lessons.title: Tracking data and play types
lessons.objective: Explain tracking data, screen assists and play-type frequencies.

payload.prompt: What is player tracking data?

options.text: Second-by-second camera and sensor data showing positions and spacing.
The number of steals a player makes per game.
A list of games a player has participated in.

explanation.correct: Right. Tracking data (from SportVU or similar systems) records player positions 25 times per second. It reveals spacing, distances and movement that box scores miss.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Tracking data is continuous positional information from cameras. It enables advanced analysis of spacing, defense and player efficiency.

payload.prompt: What is a play-type analysis?

options.text: Categorizing possessions (pick-and-roll, iso, post-up) to measure efficiency.
Identifying the type of shot a player takes.
Counting how many fouls are called.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Play-type analysis categorizes possessions: 'Iso' efficiency, 'Pick-and-roll ball handler' efficiency, 'Spot-up three' efficiency, etc.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Play-type analysis groups possessions by offensive action and measures efficiency. It shows which plays work best for a team.

payload.prompt: What does a high contested-shot rate mean?

options.text: A high percentage of a player or team's shots are defended closely (defender within 2-3 feet), suggesting tough shot-taking or poor spacing.
The player is fouled on most of their shots.
The team is winning its games closely.

explanation.correct: Right. High contested-shot rate means tough looks. A scorer with high contested rate but still shoots well is elite (he makes tough shots).
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Contested shots have a defender close by. High contested rates can mean tough offense or poor spacing. Efficiency matters given the contest.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: He is elite at rim deterrence even though he does not get many blocks.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: His presence near the basket forces opponents to avoid driving and alter shots, affecting their shots without recording blocks.
He fouls opponents constantly.
He steals the ball often.
He is very tall and intimidating.

payload.translation: She is noting that his defensive presence (body position, size, awareness) deters drives and changes shot quality even without blocks recorded.

followUps.line: So blocks do not tell the whole story.
followUps.why: You recognize that rim protection is more than blocks; presence matters.

followUps.line: His tracking data must show it.
followUps.why: A good follow-up noting that movement data reveals the full defensive impact.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rim deterrence is a player's ability to scare opponents into worse shots without necessarily getting blocks.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Their play-type distribution is bad, too much iso.

payload.question: What is she noting?

options.text: The team runs too many isolation plays instead of ball-movement actions, hurting spacing and forcing low-efficiency one-on-one shots.
The players are isolated from their families.
The team has no bench players.
The players are sitting alone on the bench.

payload.translation: She is saying the offense runs too many isolation plays (one player attacking alone) instead of screens and ball movement that generate better shots.

followUps.why: You recognize that ball movement is more efficient than iso-heavy offense.
A good follow-up identifying what the offense should use instead.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Play-type distribution shows whether an offense relies on isos, pick-and-rolls, spot-ups or other actions.

lessons.title: Eye test vs numbers
lessons.objective: Use stats to ask better questions instead of ending arguments.

payload.prompt: Should you trust a player's stellar 42% three-point shooting in the playoffs?

situation.narrative: A player is shooting 42% from three in the playoffs so far (about 40 attempts). Last season he shot 34% from three over a full season.

facts.label: Defense
facts.value: Playoff defense is tougher than regular season

options.label: It is a small sample; regress toward 34-35%
options.consequence: You recognize the playoffs are small samples. A hot stretch of 40 attempts is real but likely to regress to career average (34%).
considerations: 40 attempts is too small to trust fully
Career rate and last season are larger samples
Variance in small samples is expected

options.label: He is on fire; trust the new rate
options.consequence: Overweighting recent performance. Small samples are noise. In the next series, he might drop to 32%.
considerations: Hot streaks happen in small samples

payload.expertNote: Sample size is the most common mistake in basketball analysis. Large samples (full season) beat small samples (one series). Use stats to ask: Is this real or noise?

payload.prompt: Why do analysts care about sample size?

options.text: Small samples (few games or shots) have high variance and do not reliably predict future performance; larger samples reduce noise.
Because bigger numbers are always better.
Because it affects the length of a season.

explanation.correct: Right. A player shooting 5-for-5 in one game is noise. 50 for 100 over a season is meaningful. A 40-attempt playoff sample sits in between.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Sample size is about variance: small samples (few games) are noisy; large samples (full season) are reliable. Use full-season stats over small stretches.

payload.prompt: What is the danger of 'clutch stats' (performance in close, late-game situations)?

options.text: The sample size is tiny, creating huge variance; a player's late-game numbers over one season may not predict future clutch performance.
Clutch performance is more important than regular season.
Only superstars can perform in clutch moments.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Late-game situations (final 5 min, within 5 pts) have tiny sample sizes. A 3-for-5 night inflates clutch stats but means little over time.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Clutch performance is real but the sample size is small. Do not weight one clutch performance too heavily; ask for season-level data.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Stats said he was the MVP, but I saw him get exposed on defense.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Stats do not capture defense. Watching revealed defensive gaps the votes missed.
Statistics are always wrong.
She saw him fouling constantly.
He is a poor defensive player overall.

payload.translation: She is noting that stats alone do not tell the story; watching the games showed defensive lapses or mismatches that the numbers missed.

followUps.line: Yeah, stats do not capture everything.
followUps.why: You recognize that numbers and eye test both matter; neither is complete.

followUps.line: But his offensive numbers were real.
followUps.why: A good follow-up: acknowledge the stat's offensive value while noting the defensive gap.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Stats are useful but incomplete. Use them with the eye test. Both matter.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: He is shooting 50% from three this season.

payload.question: What would you ask first?

options.text: How many attempts is that on? On 20 attempts it is noise; on 200 it is real. Sample size tells you whether to trust the number.
Is he a good player?
How many games has he played?
Does his team win?

payload.translation: Before believing the 50% rate, you need to know the sample size (attempts). 20 attempts = noise. 200 attempts = elite shooting.

followUps.line: Yeah, I need to know how many he shot.
followUps.why: You recognize that sample size is the first question when hearing a stat.
A good follow-up asking for the context that sample size provides.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Always ask sample size first. A 50% three-rate on 20 attempts is different from 200 attempts.

payload.title: Stats vs. eye test
payload.setting: Texting after watching your crush's team play.

exchanges.theirMessage: The stats do not match what I saw in the game.

replies.text: Stats are one piece. What did you see?
replies.theirResponse: He had 20 points but was sluggish on defense.
replies.coachNote: You balanced stats and eye test. Well done.

replies.theirResponse: Not really, his numbers looked fine to me.
replies.coachNote: Dismissing stats entirely is wrong. Both matter.

replies.theirResponse: Oh, I did not think about that.
replies.coachNote: Good: offering a stat to bridge the gap.
